question: A chart of US high-school graduation rates, like one the White House posted in 2015. The rise looks huge. Where's the trick?
answer: In the axis, which starts at 77%. Drawn from zero the rise is still real: 7 more pupils in every 100 finishing school. No bar shows whether they learned more, and over those years national test scores of final-year pupils did not rise. A diploma counts years in a classroom, not skills.
move: When a pass rate climbs, ask whether the bar to pass moved too.
ask: When a success rate improves, do I ask whether the test changed as well as the people?

scene.headline: Graduation rate soars to a record
scene.honest: Up 7 points in eight years: 79% to 86%
scene.label: US high-school graduation rate
scene.found: Yes: the axis starts at 77%, so 7 points look like a leap.
scene.miss: That part is fair. Look at where the bars begin.

misses.marks: The rates on the bars are right. Their lengths aren't.
misses.headline: It was a record. The drawing makes it look like a rocket.

scene.name: Axis cut at 77%
scene.lesson: From zero, 79% to 86% is a steady climb. Find where the axis starts before you read it.

reference: National Center for Education Statistics, Public High School Graduation Rates (adjusted cohort graduation rate, 2010–11 to 2018–19), Condition of Education; NAEP 2019 Mathematics and Reading, Grade 12; Hanushek & Woessmann, The Knowledge Capital of Nations, MIT Press, 2015
